slide_text: Part 2: Inventing Grayscale
Before coding think first. A pixel has R=200, G=50, B=50. You need a single gray value. Should it be closer to 200 (because red is high) or closer to 100 (the average of all three)?

fragments.text: Neither answer is wrong it depends on what you mean by brightness. Let s try the simplest idea first and see if it s good enough.

slide_text: Now experiment. Display your result. It looks okay. But try this thought experiment: Imagine a pure green pixel and a pure red pixel . Both produce the same gray value: [math]. But does green look as bright as red to your eyes?

fragments.text: Try it look at a green square and a red square of equal RGB magnitude on your screen. Green looks much brighter. Our simple average treats them the same, but human vision doesn t.

slide_text: Exercise 2.2: Can you find weights [math] (that sum to 1) so that the grayscale conversion matches how bright things look to your eyes? Hint Green should get the biggest weight (eyes are most sensitive to green), blue the smallest. Try 0.3, 0.6, 0.1 as a starting point.

fragments.text: [code block] [code block]

slide_text: If you landed near R 0.3 + G 0.6 + B 0.1 , you just rediscovered the formula that TV engineers settled on in 1953: [math] This is the ITU-R BT.601 luminosity standard. It matches human vision because our eyes have far more green-sensitive cone cells than red or blue ones.

fragments.text: For the rest of this chapter, we ll use this as our : [code block]

slide_text: Quick Check: Why does the standard formula give green the largest weight (0.587)? A. Green light has the most energy B. The human eye is most sensitive to green C. There are more green pixels in most images D. It s arbitrary any weights work equally well

fragments.text: Answer: B. Human vision has peak sensitivity in the green range, so green contributes more to perceived brightness.

Before coding paper exercise. Here s a row of pixels: [code block] There s clearly an edge between the dark region (50) and the bright region (200). How would you compute a number that s big where there s an edge and small where it s flat?

fragments.text: Idea: For each pixel, subtract its left neighbor from its right neighbor. Where the image is flat, the difference is near zero. At an edge, it s large. [code block] The big numbers (150) mark the edge!

slide_text: Experiment gallery. For each kernel below, predict what it does before running it. Write your prediction, then check: [code block]

fragments.text: Identity. Only the center pixel survives (multiplied by 1). Output = input. It does nothing but it confirms your works!

slide_text: [code block]

fragments.text: Sharpening. The center has weight 5 and the neighbors have 1. This boosts the center pixel relative to its neighbors the opposite of blurring. Edges get crisper, details pop.
Notice the weights sum to 1 (5 4 = 1). What would happen if they summed to more than 1? Less than 1? Try it!

fragments.text: Horizontal edge detector (Sobel-y). Negative weights on top, positive on bottom. It measures the brightness difference between top and bottom rows highlighting horizontal edges.

slide_text: Experiment: Try reversing the order detect edges first, then blur: [code block] Display both. Which gives cleaner edges? Which preserves finer detail? Why does the order matter?
The big insight. In all your experiments, you chose the kernel weights: all-1/9 for blur, Sobel for edges, your custom designs. What if a computer could learn the best weights from examples?

fragments.text: That s exactly what a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) does. It starts with random kernel weights and adjusts them using gradient descent until the kernels produce features that solve the task detecting cats, reading handwriting, diagnosing X-rays. The function you wrote is the core operation of modern computer vision.
